2 — Chinese cohort (genus level): the clean case–control comparison

Group 6

2026-06-02

1. Libraries

library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)

2. Load and filter to China

From the previous file, we have provided arguments as to why we only will look at the chinese cohort. Therefore loading the object and instantly filtering so we only have the chinese cohort data.

load("project/data/D003924_Diabetes_Mellitus,_T/genus/D003924_phyloseq_updated_genus.RData")
ps <- subset_samples(pylsq, Project.ID == "PRJNA422434")
rm(pylsq)

ps
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 58 taxa and 359 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 359 samples by 12 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 58 taxa by 6 taxonomic ranks ]
## phy_tree()    Phylogenetic Tree: [ 58 tips and 27 internal nodes ]
table(sample_data(ps)$Disease.MESH.ID)
## 
## D003924 D006262 
##     187     172

Now the above shows that we have 359 samples and still 58 taxa on genus level. We can also observe a more even distribution of healthy/sick.

alpha <- estimate_richness(ps, measures = c("Shannon", "Simpson")) |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id")

meta <- sample_data(ps) |>
  data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id")

alpha_div <- inner_join(alpha, meta, by = "sample_id") |>
  mutate(Disease = ifelse(Disease.MESH.ID == "D003924", "T2D", "Healthy"))

3. Metadata / covariate balance between disease groups

Before testing we check whether the disease groups are balanced on the covariates (sex, recent antibiotic use, age). Any imbalance is a potential confounder. These we can adjust for in file 3.

Firstly, sex imbalance?

table(alpha_div$Disease, alpha_div$Sex)
##          
##           Female Male
##   Healthy     81   91
##   T2D         68  119
chisq.test(table(alpha_div$Disease, alpha_div$Sex))
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction
## 
## data:  table(alpha_div$Disease, alpha_div$Sex)
## X-squared = 3.8178, df = 1, p-value = 0.05071

Not significant. why this test?

Now, recent antibiotics use?

table(alpha_div$Disease, alpha_div$Recent.antibiotics.use, useNA = "ifany")
##          
##             N
##   Healthy 172
##   T2D     187

None. Perfect.

Now checking age.

alpha_div |>
  mutate(Host.age = as.numeric(Host.age)) |>
  group_by(Disease) |>
  summarise(median_age = median(Host.age, na.rm = TRUE),
            IQR_age    = IQR(Host.age, na.rm = TRUE),
            n          = dplyr::n(),
            .groups = "drop")
## # A tibble: 2 × 4
##   Disease median_age IQR_age     n
##   <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl> <int>
## 1 Healthy         44      19   172
## 2 T2D             55      19   187
wilcox.test(as.numeric(Host.age) ~ Disease.MESH.ID, data = alpha_div)
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  as.numeric(Host.age) by Disease.MESH.ID
## W = 22913, p-value = 3.511e-12
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

Somewhat big difference in median age. 44 and 55. Significant result. Potential confounder.

Plotting it.

alpha_div |>
  mutate(Host.age = as.numeric(Host.age)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Disease, Host.age, fill = Disease)) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3, size = 0.7) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Healthy" = "#56B4E9", "T2D" = "#E74C3C")) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Host age", title = "Age by disease (Chinese cohort)")

Now BMI. It is missing for most samples, so this is only on the complete cases.

alpha_div |>
  mutate(BMI = as.numeric(BMI)) |>
  group_by(Disease) |>
  summarise(median_BMI = median(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
            IQR_BMI    = IQR(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_with_BMI = sum(!is.na(BMI)),
            n          = dplyr::n(),
            .groups = "drop")
## # A tibble: 2 × 5
##   Disease median_BMI IQR_BMI n_with_BMI     n
##   <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>      <int> <int>
## 1 Healthy       22.2    6.48         74   172
## 2 T2D           20.9    5.67         77   187
wilcox.test(as.numeric(BMI) ~ Disease.MESH.ID, data = alpha_div)
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  as.numeric(BMI) by Disease.MESH.ID
## W = 3107.5, p-value = 0.3368
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

172 healthy - 74 has BMI metadata 187 sick - 77 has BMI metadata

On the samples with BMI metadata the p = 0.34 shows that BMI does not differ significantly between the groups.

4. Sequencing depth

Does alpha diversity correlate with sequencing depth?

wilcox.test(Nr..reads.sequenced ~ Disease.MESH.ID, data = alpha_div)
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  Nr..reads.sequenced by Disease.MESH.ID
## W = 20041, p-value = 5.582e-05
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

From this test we find that sequencing depth differs between the meshids. (p-value = 5.582e-05)

We then need to test if it correalates with alpha diversity.

cor.test(alpha_div$Nr..reads.sequenced, alpha_div$Shannon, method = "spearman")
## 
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
## 
## data:  alpha_div$Nr..reads.sequenced and alpha_div$Shannon
## S = 7262340, p-value = 0.2711
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##        rho 
## 0.05822349
ggplot(alpha_div, aes(x = Nr..reads.sequenced, y = Shannon, color = Disease)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Healthy" = "#56B4E9", "T2D" = "#E74C3C")) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Reads sequenced (log10)", y = "Shannon",
       title = "Sequencing depth vs Shannon diversity (Chinese cohort)")

Not significantly. Good. So any difference in alpha diversity is not an artefact of sequencing depth.

5. Alpha diversity by disease

Now looking at same alpha diversity measures as in file 1 to check if it’s different when we now only have the chineses cohort in the data.

alpha_div |>
  pivot_longer(c(Shannon, Simpson), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Disease, y = value, fill = Disease)) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3, size = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Healthy" = "#56B4E9", "T2D" = "#E74C3C")) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Alpha diversity",
         title = "Alpha diversity by disease (Chinese cohort, genus level)")

Testing if still significantly different.

wilcox.test(Shannon ~ Disease.MESH.ID, data = alpha_div)
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  Shannon by Disease.MESH.ID
## W = 19144, p-value = 0.001829
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
wilcox.test(Simpson ~ Disease.MESH.ID, data = alpha_div)
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  Simpson by Disease.MESH.ID
## W = 19103, p-value = 0.002106
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
alpha_div |>
  group_by(Disease) |>
  summarise(median_Shannon = median(Shannon),
            median_Simpson = median(Simpson),
            .groups = "drop")
## # A tibble: 2 × 3
##   Disease median_Shannon median_Simpson
##   <chr>            <dbl>          <dbl>
## 1 Healthy           1.54          0.686
## 2 T2D               1.60          0.715

Still significant however less than with the full dataset. This remains surprising.

6. Beta diversity by disease

Now investigating beta diversity. (Bray Curtis)

ps_rel    <- transform_sample_counts(ps, function(x) x / sum(x))
bray_dist <- distance(ps_rel, method = "bray")
ord_bray  <- ordinate(ps_rel, method = "PCoA", distance = bray_dist)
sample_df <- sample_data(ps_rel) |> data.frame()

Plotting PCoA of beta diversity colored by meshid.

plot_ordination(ps_rel, ord_bray, color = "Disease.MESH.ID") +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_ellipse(level = 0.95) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("D006262" = "#56B4E9", "D003924" = "#E74C3C"),
                     labels = c("D006262" = "Healthy", "D003924" = "T2D"),
                     name   = "Disease") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Bray–Curtis PCoA — disease (Chinese cohort)")

Not a lot to conclude. Maybe a small difference, but no clean seperation.

Let’s test this. Frsit permanova, then betadisper.

adonis2(bray_dist ~ Disease.MESH.ID, data = sample_df, permutations = 999)
## Permutation test for adonis under reduced model
## Permutation: free
## Number of permutations: 999
## 
## adonis2(formula = bray_dist ~ Disease.MESH.ID, data = sample_df, permutations = 999)
##           Df SumOfSqs      R2      F Pr(>F)    
## Model      1    1.358 0.01863 6.7759  0.001 ***
## Residual 357   71.552 0.98137                  
## Total    358   72.910 1.00000                  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Permanova is significant, F=6.78 and p = 0.001. Healthy/sick differs in composition. Disease explains only 1.8% of community variation.

Checking betadeisper

disp_disease <- betadisper(bray_dist, sample_df$Disease.MESH.ID)
anova(disp_disease)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: Distances
##            Df Sum Sq  Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
## Groups      1 0.0338 0.033824  1.4089  0.236
## Residuals 357 8.5709 0.024008

Is it

plot(disp_disease, main = "Dispersion by disease")
